passage: After the talk at the university in Manchester, Daniel found two classmates near the coffee machine. "Can I ask you something? What was unclear?" Mateo thought for a moment. "I liked it. But I only understood what you found when you got to the last slide. Before that I was guessing." The other listener nodded. Daniel felt a small sting, then curiosity. The main result had been sitting in the final minute, behind all the methods. That evening Daniel opened the slides, moved the result to slide three, and marked it with a big number. Next time the talk would start with the answer and then explain how it was reached. Mateo received a message: "Thanks. Very useful."

qa.q: Where in the talk had the main result been?
qa.a: The main result had been in the final minute, on the last slide.

qa.q: What did Daniel feel on hearing that the result came too late?
qa.a: Daniel felt a small sting first and then curiosity, which led to changing the slides.

qa.q: What other approach could help Daniel check the change, and why?
qa.a: Daniel could ask the same two listeners to hear the new order, because they can say if the point arrives earlier.

qa.q: How might Mateo see the talk before the result was moved?
qa.a: Mateo said the listening was like guessing, so the audience was probably lost until the last slide. 🙂

grounding: After a talk, a student asks two listeners what was unclear, learns the result was buried and moves it earlier next time.

In the corridor outside Seminar Room 2, Ayesha caught Raghav and Nidhi before they left for lunch. 'Two minutes? What was unclear in my talk?'
Raghav hesitated. 'Honestly? I didn't know what you found until the second-last slide.'
Nidhi nodded. 'You spent ages on the method. When the result came, I'd stopped paying attention.'
Ayesha felt a flash of annoyance. She'd worked hard on that method section. For a second she wanted to defend it. Then she thought about what she'd want as a listener, and wrote in her notebook: 'Result buried. Move it up.'
Two weeks later, at the next department seminar, her second slide said, in big letters: 'Reading aloud to toddlers increased their word count by 30% in eight weeks.' The method came after, shorter. When she looked out, Raghav gave her a thumbs-up.

qa.q: What did Ayesha write in her notebook?
How did Ayesha feel when told the result was buried, and what did she do with it?
qa.a: She felt a flash of annoyance and wanted to defend the method, but chose to think like a listener and note the change.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha ask listeners next time?
qa.a: Ask them to say the main finding in one sentence, to check it came through.

qa.q: How does Raghav experience the next seminar?
qa.a: Raghav hears the main result on the second slide and shows approval with a thumbs-up.

grounding: Shows a student asking two listeners what was unclear, learning the result was buried, and putting it near the start of the next talk.

Subject: Thank you for the honest feedback
Dear Sarita,
Thank you for staying back after my presentation on Thursday to tell me what didn't work. I'll admit, when you said you only understood the point in the last minute, part of me felt stung. I'd spent a week on those slides.
But you were right, and so was Pranjal when I asked him the same thing. I looked at the talk again: the key finding, that the new bus timings cut waiting time by a third, was on slide 14 of 15. Everything before it was background and method.
So for the conference next month I've moved it to slide 2. The method now comes after, in four slides instead of nine. I've also added a closing slide that repeats the finding in one line.
Would you be willing to watch a practice run next Friday? I'd value your eyes on it again.
Jahnavi

qa.q: On which slide was the key finding?
How did Jahnavi feel when Sarita said the point only came in the last minute?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt stung, having spent a week on the slides, but came round to seeing the feedback was right.

qa.q: What else could Jahnavi do at the practice run?
qa.a: Ask Sarita and Pranjal to state the main finding in one line afterwards, to check it now comes through early.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sarita is likely pleased that the honesty was taken well and used, and valued enough to be asked back.

grounding: Shows a student asking listeners what was unclear, learning the key finding was buried, and moving it near the start for the next talk.
